snippet.title: The Rise and Fall of America’s Steam King: Baldwin’s Dark Secrets
snippet.description:
Once, it was the most powerful locomotive builder in the world. For decades, Baldwin Locomotive Works dominated American railroads, producing thousands of steam engines that powered the nation’s growth.

Founded in 1831 and based in Philadelphia, Baldwin became a symbol of American industrial strength. By the early 20th century, it was the largest locomotive manufacturer on Earth. Its steam engines hauled freight, passengers, and even military equipment across continents.

But then everything changed.

The rise of diesel technology, aggressive competition from companies like General Motors (through its Electro-Motive Division), and internal management mistakes pushed Baldwin into a slow and painful decline. While others adapted quickly to diesel-electric locomotives, Baldwin hesitated — and paid the price.

By the 1950s, the once-mighty steam giant was struggling. Mergers, layoffs, shrinking orders, and mounting losses followed. Eventually, the empire that helped build America collapsed.

This is the dark story of ambition, innovation, resistance to change — and the fall of a titan.

If you love forgotten American history, industrial mysteries, and business rise-and-fall stories, this is one you can’t miss.

snippet.title: Blockbuster’s Final Act: The Systematic Destruction of a Global Home Entertainment Titan
snippet.description:
Once a giant of home entertainment, Blockbuster LLC dominated movie nights across the world. With thousands of stores, millions of loyal customers, and a brand that defined an era, it seemed unstoppable. But today, it stands as one of the most famous business collapses in modern history.

In this video, Blockbuster’s Final Act: The Systematic Destruction of a Global Home Entertainment Titan, we uncover the real reasons behind its dramatic downfall. From missed opportunities and poor leadership decisions to its failure to adapt to digital transformation, this is a story of how a market leader lost everything.

Whenever financial markets have a little whoopsie daisy and require government intervention to prevent further losses, there is one line that is repeated more than any other.
Yeah that’s right, we can’t let the consequences of our own actions go too far, because the retirement of millions of regular people are directly dependent on the performance of these financial assets.
And well… they kind of have a point… 
Since the year 2000 the number of people actively contributing to investment based retirement accounts has more than doubled over the same time in which defined benefit schemes have more than halved.
At the end of last year, here in America alone we collectively had almost fifty trillion dollars worth of assets tucked away into retirement accounts, with all but 13 trillion of that being directly tied to the performance of financial markets. 
That is only slightly less than the collective value of our entire residential real estate market, and voters are equally defensive of it. 
People don’t want their homes to lose value, and likewise they want to make sure that at the end of their careers they will have something to retire on…
But this logical self interest has created some perverse incentives for the entire financial industry by making hopeful retirees the ultimate bag holders for when things start to go wrong. 
Whether its private credit, private equity, BDCs, Mortgage Backed Securities or Residential REITS, if there is an asset that is starting to go bad, then this practically unlimited pool of cash has become a great escape mechanism to bail out flailing sectors because they know that if anything goes wrong the government will be there to bail them out in turn… 
This has created a weird scenario where retirement savings must simultaneously be protected at all costs while also taking on morally hazardous amounts of risk.
It’s not great, but at the very least it has empowered people to take charge of their own financial destiny right? Well we will get to that… 
But before we do, we also need to address some good news, which is that America is far from the worst offender in this whole game…

snippet.title: Who Really Controls The Internet? (The Undersea Monopoly)
snippet.description:
We are told that the internet lives in the cloud. We are told it's a decentralized, virtual space floating above us. But the brutal geopolitical reality is that the internet is physical, incredibly fragile, and buried at the bottom of the ocean.

Over 99% of all transcontinental data traffic—from global banking transactions to military communications—flows through a hidden network of undersea fiber-optic cables. And right now, a quiet monopoly is taking place. Tech giants like Google, Meta, Amazon, and Microsoft are no longer just software companies—they are buying up the physical backbone of global communication.

In this video, we dive deep into the freezing waters of the Pacific and Atlantic to dissect the massive infrastructure, the corporate monopolies, and the terrifying national security choke points that actually control the modern digital world.

🌆 Finally, the Greater Tokyo metro economy produces over $2 trillion in output, rivaling entire G7 countries like Canada.

Last year, the amount of money spent on lobbying hit a record $5.24 billion dollars at the federal level alone… and well… I don’t know if you realized, but there weren't even any major federal elections in 2025. 
When you factor in the upcoming midterms, state and local level lobbying in addition to all of the money spent outside of officially disclosed channels, the volume of cash that is… uhh “enabling” the law making process is going to eclipse 11 figures within America alone this year… and by all accounts it’s going to be a great investment… 
A cambridge university report found that out of 1,779 policy issues passed during their study, the preferences of economic elites and special business interests had a significant influence on policy outcomes which wasn’t really the shocking part… 
The shocking part was that the preferences of average citizens had effectively no measurable influence, even in large groups that were extremely politically active. Oh and this study was done in 2014, when total political spending was less than a quarter of what it is today… 
Part of the reason WHY that spending has become so ludicrous is not because the money is being used to circumvent the will of the people, (that battle was won long ago), it’s instead become a spending battle between OTHER lobbyists to see whose special interests take precedence over the lessor donors… 
but even if we somehow reformed this in its entirety tomorrow, we only need to look to other countries to see that it’s probably not going to fix all of our problems… 
Oh and of course… this is all assuming that everybody was actually playing by those rules in the first place…

snippet.title: Schaefer Beer: The Rise and Fall of America’s Forgotten Beer Giant
snippet.description:
For more than a century, F. & M. Schaefer Brewing Company stood as one of America’s most successful and recognizable beer brands. Founded in New York in the 1840s, the company grew into a massive brewing empire with iconic advertising and loyal customers across the Northeast.

At its peak, Schaefer was producing millions of barrels of beer every year and competing with industry giants like Anheuser-Busch and Pabst Brewing Company. The brand became famous for its slogan, “Schaefer is the one beer to have when you're having more than one.”

But the brewing world was changing.

As consolidation swept through the industry in the 1960s and 1970s, traditional family-run breweries began to disappear. Corporate buyouts, Wall Street financing, rising costs, and fierce competition from national brands reshaped the American beer landscape.

Schaefer’s story is not just about beer — it’s about how financial markets, corporate mergers, and shifting consumer tastes transformed an entire industry.

In this documentary, we explore the rise of Schaefer, its massive expansion, the financial decisions that changed its fate, and how Wall Street ultimately played a role in dismantling one of America’s most iconic brewing empires.

This is the story of innovation, ambition, corporate power — and the slow collapse of a legendary American beer brand.

Amidst all of the chaos of last week, the world's largest asset manager (blackrock) quietly announced something that should be making a lot of people extremely worried. 
They would be limiting withdrawals on one of their flagship private credit funds that currently has (or at least had) 26 billion dollars worth of assets under management. 
Now I know that there is a lot going on in the world right now and compared to some of the headlines we have seen in the past week this might sound pretty minor, but a hiccup like this in these markets could genuinely be the sign, symptom and cause of something much scarier. 
On one hand, people pulling money out of these kinds of funds is a sign that things are not going well amongst even the most high end investors. 
On the other hand, the fact that they can’t get their money out is a symptom of people predicting things are about to get much worse… 
And on the third hand, a shocking amount of everyday businesses have been propped up by the easy lending done by firms like this… If their money stops flowing, it could easily cause much larger knock on effects throughout the real economy in extremely direct ways. 
But before we get too hyperbolic, it’s important to understand exactly what these funds were supposed to do and more importantly what they have actually been doing, because depending on your interpretation of this business model, this headline is either little more than dumb investors not understanding what they invested in… or it’s the modern equivalent of a bank run. 
The total debt outstanding in this highly risky class of finance is now over 2 trillion dollars (and that’s only what we actually know of), either way that’s almost twice as much as the 1.3 trillion dollars in subprime mortgage lending done in 2008, and with an alarming number of parallels it’s clear to see why some people are getting nervous… 
Now that alone is… not great… but it gets worse…
If one Blackrock fund really was the only fund having problems it could probably just be written off as (a concerning but ultimately) isolated incident, unfortunately though, this week's announcement was just the latest (and so far) largest example of major issues in these multi trillion dollar private markets…

snippet.title: From Regional Favorite to Forgotten Name — Wiedemann’s Collapse
snippet.description:
or decades, Wiedemann Brewery was a proud Midwestern institution, rooted in German brewing tradition and beloved across the Ohio Valley. Founded in the 19th century in Newport, Kentucky, Wiedemann built a loyal following with affordable, quality beer and strong regional identity.

But the brewing industry was changing.

As national brands expanded and consolidation swept through the market, smaller regional breweries found themselves under pressure. When corporate interests stepped in, what was presented as a “rescue” would ultimately lead to something far more devastating.

In this documentary, we uncover how mergers, shifting consumer tastes, industry consolidation, and strategic decisions led to the collapse of Wiedemann. Was it inevitable… or avoidable?

This is the story of how a local favorite became a casualty of big business — and what its fall reveals about the transformation of America’s beer industry.
